title: Cisco CyberOps Associate (200-201): The SOC Analyst Cert for 2026
body: Cisco CyberOps Associate (200-201 CBROPS) is the entry-level security operations certification Cisco built specifically for SOC analyst roles. The exam covers five domains in approximately 95–100 questions over 120 minutes and costs $330 USD, with no formal prerequisites and a three-year validity period. Five domains are tested: Security Concepts (20%), Security Monitoring (25%), Host-Based Analysis (20%), Network Intrusion Analysis (20%), and Security Policies and Procedures (15%). Unlike broad-coverage security certs such as CompTIA Security+, the CyberOps Associate is purpose-built for the day-to-day analyst workflow: monitoring SIEM alerts, triaging events, reading packet captures, analyzing host logs, and executing incident response playbooks. Entry-level SOC roles held by CyberOps-certified analysts average $65k–$90k in 2026; experienced analysts at Tier 2 and above reach $95k–$125k in North American markets.

The Security Monitoring domain at 25% is the exam's heaviest section and covers the core SOC workflow in depth. Candidates must understand SIEM architecture — how log sources feed into a correlation engine, how alert rules are structured, and how to distinguish true positives from false positives in a high-volume alert queue. Network traffic analysis using Wireshark and tcpdump is tested at the packet level: TCP anomalies, SYN flood signatures, port scanning patterns, HTTP injection indicators, and DNS tunneling behavior. NetFlow and IPFIX analysis for detecting C2 beaconing and data exfiltration are also covered. The Host-Based Analysis domain adds Windows and Linux endpoint forensics: reading Windows Event Logs by Event ID (4624, 4625, 4688, 4697), identifying malware persistence mechanisms on both platforms, and understanding what EDR telemetry reveals about attacker activity. Network Intrusion Analysis covers IDS/IPS rule interpretation using Snort-style syntax, NIDS versus HIDS placement and blind spots, and how firewall logs are correlated with SIEM alerts to reconstruct attack timelines.

The Security Concepts domain establishes the foundational model: CIA triad, vulnerability versus threat versus risk, cryptography fundamentals (symmetric/asymmetric, hashing, PKI), malware taxonomy (ransomware, rootkits, worms, trojans), and the MITRE ATT&CK framework as the taxonomy for categorizing attacker techniques. The Security Policies and Procedures domain covers the incident response lifecycle (Preparation → Identification → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned), data classification, regulatory context (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR), SOC role hierarchy and escalation paths (Tier 1 triage, Tier 2 investigation, Tier 3 hunt), and chain-of-custody procedures for digital evidence. Cisco provides a free two-part CyberOps Associate curriculum through Cisco Networking Academy (NetAcad) covering all five domains with embedded Wireshark labs, Security Onion exercises, and module assessments — the official free preparation path.

The natural progression after CyberOps Associate is Cisco CyberOps Professional, which requires the CCNP-level core exam 350-701 SCOR plus one concentration exam. Alternatively, candidates who specialize in threat hunting, digital forensics, or incident command frequently pursue GIAC credentials (GCIH, GCIA, GCED) or ISC2 SSCP as their next cert. CyberOps Associate holders with CCNA experience have the strongest preparation baseline — the two exams share TCP/IP and network protocol fundamentals while diverging completely at the analysis layer. Candidates without networking backgrounds typically extend their preparation by 4–6 weeks compared to CCNA holders. For candidates choosing between CyberOps Associate and CompTIA Security+: CyberOps Associate is deeper in SOC-specific monitoring and analysis skills; Security+ is broader in coverage and meets DoD 8140 compliance requirements. Many SOC-track professionals eventually hold both.
